message.content:
The sea usually looks **blue**—that’s because water absorbs colors at the red end of the spectrum more strongly than those at the blue end, so when sunlight hits the ocean surface most of the visible light that gets reflected back into our eyes is blue.  

However, the exact hue you see depends on several factors:

| Factor | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| Depth & clarity | Deeper, clearer waters appear darker‑bluer; shallow or murky areas may look greenish or even brownish if there’s algae or sediment. |
| Sun angle | At sunrise/sunset the sky casts warmer tones onto the water, giving it pinks, oranges, or reds. |
| Weather & clouds | Overcast skies reduce contrast, making the sea seem grayish or muted. |
| Surface conditions | Calm surfaces reflect the sky, often mirroring its blues/whites; waves scatter light differently, sometimes creating turquoise or teal patches. |

So while “blue” is the classic description, the sea’s color can shift across a palette from deep navy to bright aqua, all thanks to how light interacts with water and what lies beneath it.
